newsitem.title: CHINA: Symbolism outweighs substance of Gore's China trip.
newsitem.headline: Symbolism outweighs substance of Gore's China trip.

text.p: Symbolism outweighed substance in U.S. Vice President Al Gore's landmark talks with Chinese leaders, but his trip and a planned exchange of presidential visits could help stabilise ties, diplomats said on Thursday.

Gore, the most senior U.S. leader to come to China since Beijing sent tanks and soldiers to crush pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989, met Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday, a day after meeting Premier Li Peng.

Both sides hailed the meetings as a vital step to smoothing the ruffled cross-Pacific relationship and an affirmation that Jiang would visit the United States in the autumn. U.S. President Bill Clinton would then visit China in 1998.
"The symbolism of Gore's visit was the main thing, I don't think either side was expecting anything substantive to come out of it," said one Western diplomat in the Chinese capital.

While Gore and his Chinese hosts appeared to make little concrete progress on issues such as trade, human rights and Taiwan that have long tormented ties, the coming presidentrial exchanges were at least likely to dampen frictions, he said.
No one wanted to see friction jeopardise a diplomatic event as vital as Jiang's Washington visit, said another diplomat.
"Unless something really big happens... both sides will cooperate in making sure that nothing goes wrong with that," he said.

Gore had made clear that allegations China tried to make illegal donations to U.S. Democratic Party politicians would not be allowed to derail the fragile rapprochement between the two Pacific powers, the diplomats said.
The Washington Post has reported that U.S. investigators warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds.

Beijing has denied the allegations, and Gore said on Wednesday an official investigation should not disrupt Sino-U.S. ties -- although he added that such illegal funding would be a serious matter if proven.

While the allegations dominated much of Gore's visit, they were unlikely to do much harm to Sino-U.S ties, not least because the scandal was at least as potentially damaging to U.S. leaders as to China's image, the diplomats said.

"It's a domestic U.S. issue... the interests of both sides coincide in keeping the temperature down," one diplomat said, although he added that U.S. sensitivity over the issue could have helped to limit progress during Gore's meetings.

"I think the visit has been fairly inconclusive partly because of American worries that if they start announcing great progress in the political relationship... the press back home will say 'Oh yes, we know how you got that'," he said.

Both Washington and Beijing remained committed to repairing their relationship after the damage suffered in 1995, when ties chilled over a private visit to the United States by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui, the diplomats said.
Taiwan, which Beijing considers a rebel province, was an issue on which no Chinese leader could afford to compromise and remained a real threat to Sino-U.S. ties, they said.
The increasing interest paid by U.S. leaders to the future of Hong Kong, which returns to Chinese rule on July 1, was another major worry for Beijing, said one diplomat.
Sino-U.S. ties remained on a rocky road after Gore's meetings, despite the friendly smiles and poetic lines he exchanged with his Chinese hosts, another diplomat said.

"Neither side, however much they might want to, is actually succeeding yet in getting the relationship onto a whole new plane," he said. "U.S.-China is like that; it's so subject to bad weather that just keeping things on track is an achievement in itself."
